# How to Test a Teaching

*AN 3.65, the Kesamutta Sutta — set 1, Before Any Doctrine*

<p class="reading-meta"><strong>Reading time:</strong> about 10 min · 1,786 words</p>

[Skip to the translation](#translation){ .reader-skip-link }

## Before you read

<div class="reader-guide" markdown="1">

### What happens

At Kesamutta, the Kālāmas tell the Buddha that visiting teachers praise their own teachings, attack the teachings of others, and leave the community unsure whom to believe.

### Central question

When teachers disagree, how can you judge which qualities and practices lead to harm and which lead to well-being?

### Main point

The Buddha says that tradition, reports, scripture, reasoning, how capable a speaker seems, and loyalty to a teacher are not enough on their own. Look at what happens when a teaching is put into practice: give up what leads to harm, and develop what leads to well-being and happiness.

### Reading tip

The text first lists ten reasons that are not enough by themselves. Then it compares greed, aversion, and delusion with their opposites. It ends with friendliness, kindness, gladness, and balance, followed by four reasons for confidence.

### This text is not saying

The text does not say that reasoning, tradition, or personal judgment are worthless. It says none of the listed grounds is enough by itself.

### Key words

<dl class="reader-guide__terms">
<dt><dfn>wholesome</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;kusala&quot; -- roughly, mentally and ethically healthy: blameless, leads to well-being, and is praised by people with good judgment.</dd>
<dt><dfn>unwholesome</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;akusala&quot; -- roughly, mentally and ethically harmful: blameworthy, leads to harm, and is criticized by people with good judgment.</dd>
<dt><dfn>those with discernment</dfn></dt>
<dd>People whose judgment is sound enough to trust as a check on your own -- not an appeal to authority, but a practical reference point.</dd>
<dt><dfn>consolation</dfn></dt>
<dd>A practical reassurance that holds up regardless of how a contested question (like what happens after death) actually turns out -- not an argument that settles the question.</dd>
</dl>

</div>

## Translation

### The Setting

So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the
Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus when he arrived at a town of
the Kālāmas called Kesamutta.

The Kālāmas of Kesamutta heard: "The recluse Gotama — a Sakyan, gone forth
from a Sakyan family — has arrived at Kesamutta. This good report has spread
about that Blessed One: 'He is indeed the Buddha, the arahant, perfectly
and fully awakened...' It is good to see such arahants."

The Kālāmas of Kesamutta went to the Buddha. Some bowed and sat to one
side; some exchanged friendly greetings and polite conversation and sat to one
side; some raised cupped palms toward the Buddha and sat to one side; some
announced their name and clan and sat to one side; some sat to one side in
silence. Seated to one side, the Kālāmas of Kesamutta said to the Buddha:

### The Kālāmas' Uncertainty

"Bhante, there are some recluses and brahmins who come to Kesamutta. They
explain and illuminate only their own doctrine, while they attack, belittle,
disparage, and mock the doctrines of others. Then other recluses and brahmins
come to Kesamutta, and they too explain and illuminate only their own doctrine,
while they attack, belittle, disparage, and mock the doctrines of others. We
are left, Bhante, with doubt and uncertainty: which of these venerable recluses
and brahmins speaks the truth, and which speaks falsely?"

"It is right, Kālāmas, for you to doubt — right for you to be uncertain. You
have become uncertain about something genuinely uncertain.

### The Ten Criteria

Come, Kālāmas. Do not go by oral transmission; do not go by lineage; do not go
by hearsay; do not go by scriptural authority; do not go by logical
argumentation; do not go by inference; do not go by thinking through the
apparent reasons; do not go by agreeing with a view after reflecting on it; do
not go by the apparent competence of a speaker; and do not think 'This recluse
is our teacher.'

But when you know for yourselves: 'These things are unwholesome, blameworthy,
criticized by those with discernment; when taken up and undertaken they lead to
harm and suffering' — then give them up.

### The Three Roots of Harm

What do you think, Kālāmas — does greed arise within a person for their welfare
or for their harm?"

"For their harm, Bhante."

"When greed seizes a person and takes over their heart, they kill living
creatures, take what is not given, go to another's partner, speak falsely, and
encourage others to do likewise. That brings them long-lasting harm and
suffering."

"Yes, Bhante."

"What do you think, Kālāmas — does aversion arise within a person for their
welfare or for their harm?"

"For their harm, Bhante."

"When aversion seizes a person and takes over their heart, they kill
living creatures, take what is not given, go to another's partner, speak
falsely, and encourage others to do likewise. That brings them long-lasting
harm and suffering."

"Yes, Bhante."

"What do you think, Kālāmas — does delusion arise within a person for their
welfare or for their harm?"

"For their harm, Bhante."

"When delusion seizes a person and takes over their heart, they kill
living creatures, take what is not given, go to another's partner, speak
falsely, and encourage others to do likewise. That brings them long-lasting
harm and suffering."

"Yes, Bhante."

"What do you think, Kālāmas — are these things wholesome or unwholesome?"

"Unwholesome, Bhante."

"Blameworthy or blameless?"

"Blameworthy, Bhante."

"Criticized or praised by those with discernment?"

"Criticized by those with discernment, Bhante."

"When taken up and undertaken, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not? How
do you see this?"

"When taken up and undertaken, they lead to harm and suffering. That is how we
see it."

"So, Kālāmas, when I said: 'Come, Kālāmas. Do not go by oral transmission; do
not go by lineage; do not go by hearsay; do not go by scriptural authority; do
not go by logical argumentation; do not go by inference; do not go by thinking
through the apparent reasons; do not go by agreeing with a view after
reflecting on it; do not go by the apparent competence of a speaker; and do not
think "This recluse is our teacher." But when you know for yourselves — "These
things are unwholesome, blameworthy, criticized by those with discernment; when
taken up and undertaken they lead to harm and suffering" — then give them up.'
That is what I said, and this is why I said it.

### The Three Roots of Welfare

Come, Kālāmas. Do not go by oral transmission; do not go by lineage; do not go
by hearsay; do not go by scriptural authority; do not go by logical
argumentation; do not go by inference; do not go by thinking through the
apparent reasons; do not go by agreeing with a view after reflecting on it; do
not go by the apparent competence of a speaker; and do not think 'This recluse
is our teacher.'

But when you know for yourselves: 'These things are wholesome, blameless,
praised by those with discernment; when taken up and undertaken they lead to
welfare and happiness' — then take them up and live accordingly.

What do you think, Kālāmas — does non-greed arise within a person for their
welfare or for their harm?"

"For their welfare, Bhante."

"When a person is free of greed, it does not overwhelm or take over their
heart. They do not kill living creatures, take what is not given, go to
another's partner, speak falsely, or encourage others to do likewise. That
brings them long-lasting welfare and happiness."

"Yes, Bhante."

"What do you think, Kālāmas — does non-aversion arise within a person for
their welfare or for their harm? ... Does non-delusion arise within a person
for their welfare or for their harm? ... Is that for their long-lasting welfare
and happiness?"

"Yes, Bhante."

"What do you think, Kālāmas — are these things wholesome or unwholesome?"

"Wholesome, Bhante."

"Blameworthy or blameless?"

"Blameless, Bhante."

"Criticized or praised by those with discernment?"

"Praised by those with discernment, Bhante."

"When taken up and undertaken, do they lead to welfare and happiness, or not?"

"When taken up and undertaken, they lead to welfare and happiness. That is how
we see it."

"So, Kālāmas, when I said: 'Come, Kālāmas. Do not go by oral transmission...
and do not think "This recluse is our teacher." But when you know for
yourselves — "These things are wholesome, blameless, praised by those with
discernment; when taken up and undertaken they lead to welfare and happiness"
— then take them up and live accordingly.' That is what I said, and this is
why I said it.

### Friendliness, Kindness, Gladness, and Dynamic Balance

That noble disciple, Kālāmas, free of coveting, free of aversive distraction,
unconfused, clearly knowing and remembering, dwells pervading one direction
with a heart filled with friendliness, likewise the second, likewise the
third, likewise the fourth — and so above, below, across, everywhere, for all
as for themselves, they dwell pervading the entire world with a heart
filled with friendliness, vast, expansive, boundless, without enmity and
without ill will.

They dwell pervading one direction with a heart filled with kindness
towards others, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth —
and so above, below, across, everywhere, for all as for themselves, they dwell
pervading the entire world with a heart filled with kindness towards
others, vast, expansive, boundless, without enmity and without ill will.

They dwell pervading one direction with a heart filled with gladness,
likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth — and so above,
below, across, everywhere, for all as for themselves, they dwell pervading the
entire world with a heart filled with gladness, vast, expansive,
boundless, without enmity and without ill will.

They dwell pervading one direction with a heart filled with dynamic
balance, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth — and so
above, below, across, everywhere, for all as for themselves, they dwell
pervading the entire world with a heart filled with dynamic balance,
vast, expansive, boundless, without enmity and without ill will.

### The Four Consolations

That noble disciple, Kālāmas, with a heart free of enmity, free of ill
will, uncorrupted and pure, wins four consolations in this very life.

'If there is another world, and if good and bad actions do bear fruit and
result — then when this body breaks up, after death, I will be reborn in a good
destination, a heavenly world.' This is the first consolation won.

'If there is no other world, and if good and bad actions do not bear fruit and
result — then in this very life I keep myself free of enmity, free of ill will,
untroubled and happy.' This is the second consolation won.

'If bad things do come to those who do bad — I have no harmful intention toward
anyone. Not doing any bad action, how could suffering reach me?' This is the
third consolation won.

'If bad things do not come to those who do bad — then I see myself pure on both
sides.' This is the fourth consolation won.

That noble disciple, Kālāmas, with a heart free of enmity, free of ill
will, uncorrupted and pure — they win these four consolations in this very
life."

"That is exactly so, Blessed One. That is exactly so, Well-Departed One. That
noble disciple, Bhante, with a heart free of enmity, free of ill will,
uncorrupted and pure, wins four consolations in this very life.

'If there is another world, and if good and bad actions do bear fruit and
result — then when this body breaks up, after death, I will be reborn in a good
destination, a heavenly world.' This is the first consolation won.

'If there is no other world, and if good and bad actions do not bear fruit and
result — then in this very life I keep myself free of enmity, free of ill will,
untroubled and happy.' This is the second consolation won.

'If bad things do come to those who do bad — I have no harmful intention toward
anyone. Not doing any bad action, how could suffering reach me?' This is the
third consolation won.

'If bad things do not come to those who do bad — then I see myself pure on both
sides.' This is the fourth consolation won.

That noble disciple, Bhante, with a heart free of enmity, free of ill
will, uncorrupted and pure — they win these four consolations in this very
life.

### Going for Refuge

Excellent, Bhante! Excellent! ... We, Bhante, go to the Buddha for
refuge, and to the Dhamma and the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. May the Buddha receive
us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forward for as long
as life lasts."

The fifth discourse is finished.

*[arahant]: Someone who has completed the path and has nothing further to do. Left untranslated; "saint" and "perfected one" both mislead.
*[aversion]: One of the three "roots" behind unwholesome action, alongside greed and delusion -- the pushback against what's unwanted or unpleasant.
*[aversive distraction]: Being pulled off track by ill will, hostility, or pushing things away.
*[Bhante]: A respectful way of addressing a senior monastic, roughly "venerable sir." Left untranslated because English has no natural equivalent.
*[bhikkhus]: Buddhist monks -- those who have left household life to practise full time. The Buddha's usual way of addressing the assembly, roughly "friends" in force.
*[Blessed One]: One of the Buddha's traditional titles, used respectfully in place of his name in these texts.
*[body]: The physical body, as distinct from speech and the mental side of experience.
*[clearly knowing]: Acting while plainly aware of what you are doing.
*[consolation]: A practical reassurance that holds up regardless of how a contested question (like what happens after death) actually turns out -- not an argument that settles the question.
*[delusion]: One of the three "roots" behind unwholesome action, alongside greed and aversion -- the confusion that keeps you from seeing what's actually happening.
*[Dhamma]: The Buddha's teaching taken as a whole -- both what he taught and the way things actually are, which the teaching describes.
*[dynamic balance]: This project's rendering of "upekkhā" (often translated "equanimity") -- a steadiness that stays engaged rather than checking out, distinct from indifference.
*[friendliness]: This project's rendering of "mettā" (often translated "loving-kindness") -- an intentionally cultivated goodwill extended outward, including to people you don't know.
*[gladness]: This project's rendering of "muditā" (often translated "sympathetic joy") -- being genuinely glad at someone else's good fortune, cultivated as a practice rather than assumed to come naturally.
*[greed]: One of the three "roots" behind unwholesome action, alongside aversion and delusion -- the acquisitive pull toward what looks satisfying.
*[heart]: This project's rendering of "citta" -- the affective or feeling side of mind: the part that takes on a mood, wants, leans, reacts, and can be gladdened, steadied, trained, and released. It is sometimes called the "heart-mind" or "feeling mind"; here "heart" does not mean merely emotion or the physical organ.
*[kindness towards others]: This project's rendering of "karuṇā" (often translated "compassion") -- an active wish for others to be free of suffering, cultivated deliberately rather than left to spontaneous feeling.
*[noble disciple]: Someone who has had the breakthrough into the path and so is no longer merely an ordinary person. It does not mean noble by birth, and does not require being a monastic.
*[non-aversion]: The absence of hostility and the reflex to push away what is unwanted. One of the three roots of wholesome action.
*[non-greed]: The absence of the grasping pull that wants to acquire, possess, or consume. One of the three roots of wholesome action.
*[remembering]: This project's rendering of "sati" -- actively keeping what matters in mind and returning to it when it is lost, not bare attention to whatever happens to be present.
*[those with discernment]: People whose judgment is sound enough to trust as a check on your own -- not an appeal to authority, but a practical reference point.
*[unwholesome]: This project's rendering of "akusala" -- roughly, mentally and ethically harmful: blameworthy, leads to harm, and is criticized by people with good judgment.
*[wholesome]: This project's rendering of "kusala" -- roughly, mentally and ethically healthy: blameless, leads to well-being, and is praised by people with good judgment.
*[world]: A common word in these texts that shifts meaning by context -- sometimes the physical cosmos beings are reborn into, sometimes (as in MN 63) a specific philosophical question about whether existence as a whole is eternal or finite. Each sutta's own framing makes clear which sense is meant.
